塔羅蓋託管屬氣鳴樂器，最早見於十五世紀匈牙利文獻，原為蘇爾奈管（zurna）變體: The tarogato is an aerophone first recorded in Hungarian documents in the fifteenth century. It began as a variant of the zurna, brought in by the Turks in the Ottoman period, and was formerly called the Turkish pipe. Before the eighteenth century it had a double reed, a conical bore and no keys, and was loud enough to serve as a battlefield signal; because it came to stand for the Rákóczi war of independence it was suppressed under the Habsburgs. At the end of the nineteenth century the Budapest instrument maker Vencel József Schunda rebuilt the modern version as a wooden instrument with a single reed and a conical bore, and kept the old name because of its nationalist image. In the twentieth century Luță Ioviță took it to the Romanian Banat, where it is called the taragot; production stopped in Hungary after the war and continued in Romania and elsewhere, and in the 1990s Hungary began making it again.
塔羅蓋託管常見於匈牙利民間音樂，也在羅馬尼亞巴納特地區以 taragot 之名流: The tarogato is common in Hungarian folk music and is also popular in the Romanian Banat under the name taragot. In opera, some houses use it in place of the offstage cor anglais for the last part of the shepherd's melody in Act III of Wagner's Tristan und Isolde. The instrument also appears in the symphonic dance bands of the early twentieth century, in free jazz and free improvisation, and on dance-pop singles.
塔羅蓋託管是歐洲匈牙利的木管氣鳴樂器，H-S分類422.212。現代型以單簧片發: The tarogato is a wooden aerophone from Hungary in Europe, H-S classification 422.212. The modern type sounds with a single reed, has a conical bore and is mostly made of grenadilla; the earlier type had a double reed and no keys. It is common in Hungarian folk music, some opera houses use it in place of the offstage cor anglais in Act III of Wagner's Tristan und Isolde, and after reaching the Romanian Banat it became popular under the name taragot; it also appears in free jazz, improvisation and pop songs.
塔羅蓋託管音色依形制與簧片而異。早期雙簧、圓錐管無鍵版本音量大而粗礪，可作戰場信: The timbre of the tarogato varies with the form and the reed. The early double-reed, keyless, conical version was loud and rough and could serve as a battlefield signal; depending on the type of reed and on a relaxed, steady tempo it can also produce a subtle, deep, soft tone. The modern version uses a single reed and a conical bore; the most common B-flat soprano type has a mournful quality, somewhere between the cor anglais and the soprano saxophone. Other sizes exist, but the source does not give their exact range or how the volume is controlled. Compared with related instruments, its single-reed sound is close to the clarinet or the saxophone, while the conical bore makes its timbre different from that of purely cylindrical pipes.
